select-all.title: Your first query
intro: A database keeps its data in tables, like spreadsheets: each row is a thing, each column a detail about it. The brick shop has two tables: `bricks` and `orders`. Look at them in the tabs on the right.
To read a table, write `SELECT`, the columns you want, `FROM` and the table name. The star `*` means every column. A query ends with a `;`.
select-all.goal: The query reads the `orders` table. Change it to show every column of the `bricks` table.
hints: Keep `SELECT * FROM` and change only the table name.
The table name is `bricks`, in lowercase, with an s.
`SELECT * FROM bricks;`
select-all.recap: `SELECT * FROM bricks;` reads every row and every column of a table.

pick-columns.title: Only the columns you need
intro: `*` is handy to discover a table, but you usually need a few columns only. List them after `SELECT`, separated by commas.
The columns appear in the result in the order you wrote them.
pick-columns.goal: Show only the `name` and the `price` of every brick, in this order.
hints: Replace the `*` with the column names.
Separate the columns with a comma: `name, price`.
`SELECT name, price FROM bricks;`
pick-columns.recap: `SELECT name, price` picks the columns, in the order you list them.

rename-columns.title: Rename a column
intro: The result columns take the names of the table columns. `AS` gives a column another name in the result, without changing the table.
A name with no spaces is the easiest: `in_stock` rather than `in stock`.
rename-columns.goal: Show the name of each brick as `brick` and its stock as `in_stock`.
hints: Write `AS` and the new name right after a column: `name AS brick`.
Rename both columns, with a comma between them.
`SELECT name AS brick, stock AS in_stock FROM bricks;`
rename-columns.recap: `AS` renames a column in the result only: the table keeps its column names.

sort-rows.title: Sort the rows
intro: Without instructions, the database returns the rows in any order. `ORDER BY` sorts them by a column, after the `FROM`.
The order is ascending (smallest first) by default. Add `DESC` after the column for descending (biggest first).
sort-rows.goal: Show the name and price of every brick, the most expensive first.
hints: Add `ORDER BY price` at the end of the query, before the `;`.
The most expensive first means descending: add `DESC`.
`SELECT name, price FROM bricks ORDER BY price DESC;`
sort-rows.recap: `ORDER BY price DESC` sorts from the biggest value to the smallest; `ASC`, the default, does the opposite.

where-number.title: Filter the rows
intro: `WHERE` keeps only the rows that match a condition. It comes after the `FROM`: `WHERE stock = 0` keeps the rows whose stock is zero.
Numbers are written as they are, with no quotes. In SQL, a single `=` compares two values.
where-number.goal: Show the name and stock of the bricks that are out of stock (a stock of 0).
hints: Add a `WHERE` line after `FROM bricks`.
The condition compares the `stock` column to `0`.
`SELECT name, stock FROM bricks WHERE stock = 0;`
where-number.recap: `WHERE stock = 0` keeps only the rows where the condition is true.

where-compare.title: More than, less than
intro: Numbers can be compared with `<` (less than), `>` (more than), `<=` (less or equal), `>=` (more or equal) and `<>` (different).
Decimal numbers are written with a dot: `0.30`.
where-compare.goal: Show the name and price of the bricks that cost 0.30 or more.
hints: `= 0.30` keeps only the bricks at exactly 0.30: you need another operator.
0.30 included means more or equal: `>=`.
`SELECT name, price FROM bricks WHERE price >= 0.30;`
where-compare.recap: `>=` includes the value itself, `>` excludes it.

where-text.title: Text needs quotes
intro: Text values are written between single quotes: `'blue'`. Without quotes, the database reads `blue` as the name of a column and complains that it does not exist.
The text must match exactly: `'blue'` and `'Blue'` are different values.
where-text.goal: Show the name and color of the `blue` bricks.
hints: Add a condition on the `color` column.
Write the color between single quotes: `'blue'`.
`SELECT name, color FROM bricks WHERE color = 'blue';`
where-text.recap: Text goes between single quotes; names of columns and tables don't.

where-like.title: Text that starts with…
intro: `=` compares the whole text: no brick is called just `'Classic'`. `LIKE` compares the text to a pattern, where `%` stands for any characters, even none.
`'Classic%'` matches every text starting with Classic, `'%2'` every text ending with 2, `'%x%'` every text containing an x.
where-like.goal: Show the name and studs of every Classic brick (their name starts with Classic).
hints: Replace `=` with `LIKE`.
Add `%` right after the word, inside the quotes.
`SELECT name, studs FROM bricks WHERE name LIKE 'Classic%';`
where-like.recap: `LIKE 'Classic%'` matches a pattern: `%` stands for any characters.

where-date.title: Dates
intro: Dates are written as text, between quotes, in the year-month-day format: `'2024-11-01'`. In this order, the earlier date is also the smaller one, so `<` means before and `>` means after.
Always use two digits for the month and the day: `'2024-11-01'`, not `'2024-11-1'`.
where-date.goal: Show the customer and date of the orders placed on November 1st, 2024 or later.
hints: Add a condition on the `ordered_on` column.
On November 1st or later means `>=` with the date `'2024-11-01'`.
`SELECT customer, ordered_on FROM orders WHERE ordered_on >= '2024-11-01';`
where-date.recap: Dates are quoted and written year-month-day: they compare like numbers, earlier is smaller.

where-and.title: Both conditions: AND
intro: `AND` joins two conditions: a row is kept only when both are true. Each condition is complete on its own: `color = 'white' AND stock > 10`.
The more conditions joined with `AND`, the fewer rows in the result.
where-and.goal: Show the `white` bricks that have more than 10 bricks in stock.
hints: Keep the condition on the color and add a second one with `AND`.
The second condition is `stock > 10`.
`SELECT name, color, stock FROM bricks WHERE color = 'white' AND stock > 10;`
where-and.recap: With `AND`, a row must match every condition.

where-or.title: One or the other: OR
intro: `OR` joins two conditions too, but a row is kept when at least one of them is true.
Repeat the column in each condition: `color = 'red' OR color = 'green'`. `color = 'red' OR 'green'` does not work.
where-or.goal: Show the `red` bricks and the `green` bricks.
hints: Add a second condition with `OR`.
The second condition is complete too: `color = 'green'`.
`SELECT name, color FROM bricks WHERE color = 'red' OR color = 'green';`
where-or.recap: With `OR`, a row must match at least one condition.

and-or.title: AND and OR together
intro: When a condition mixes them, `AND` goes first, like × before + in maths. `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`.
Parentheses choose the order: `(a OR b) AND c` checks the `OR` first.
and-or.goal: The query returns 4 bricks, but it should only return the red or yellow bricks that cost less than 0.25. Fix it.
hints: Right now, every red brick is kept, whatever its price: the price only applies to the yellow ones.
Put parentheses around the two colors.
`WHERE (color = 'red' OR color = 'yellow') AND price < 0.25`
and-or.recap: `AND` goes before `OR`: add parentheses whenever you mix them, so the query does what you mean.

where-in.title: One of a list: IN
intro: Several `OR` on the same column get long. `IN` checks that a value is one of a list: `customer IN ('Ana', 'Ben')` means `customer = 'Ana' OR customer = 'Ben'`.
The list goes between parentheses, its values separated by commas.
where-in.goal: Show the customer and quantity of the orders from Ana, Chloe and Farid.
hints: Add `WHERE customer IN (...)`.
Each name is text: between quotes, separated by commas.
`WHERE customer IN ('Ana', 'Chloe', 'Farid')`
where-in.recap: `IN (...)` is a short way to write several `OR` on the same column.

date-between.title: A period: BETWEEN
intro: `BETWEEN` keeps the values from a start to an end, both included: `quantity BETWEEN 10 AND 30` means `quantity >= 10 AND quantity <= 30`.
It works on numbers, and on dates written year-month-day.
date-between.goal: Show the name and date of the bricks added from March 1st to June 30th, 2024.
hints: Add a condition on `added_on` with `BETWEEN ... AND ...`.
Both dates are quoted text: `'2024-03-01'` and `'2024-06-30'`.
`WHERE added_on BETWEEN '2024-03-01' AND '2024-06-30'`
date-between.recap: `BETWEEN` includes both ends of the range.

date-parts.title: Part of a date
intro: `strftime` extracts a part of a date: `strftime('%Y', added_on)` gives the year, `'%m'` the month, `'%d'` the day.
Careful with the types: the result is text, so compare it to text, `'2023'`, not to the number `2023`.
date-parts.goal: Show the name and date of the bricks added in 2023.
hints: Add a condition comparing `strftime('%Y', added_on)` to the year.
The year is text: write it between quotes.
`WHERE strftime('%Y', added_on) = '2023'`
date-parts.recap: `strftime` returns text: `'2023'` matches, the number `2023` does not.

insert-row.title: Add a row: INSERT
intro: `INSERT INTO` adds a row to a table: the list of columns, then `VALUES` with one value per column, in the same order.
Each value must have the right type: numbers as they are, text and dates between quotes.
insert-row.goal: Add the green Classic 1x2 brick (id 11) to the `bricks` table: fix the values so the query runs.
hints: The database stops at `Classic 1x2`: text needs quotes.
`'green'` is text too, and so is the date: without quotes, `2024-11-09` is a subtraction.
insert-row.recap: Numbers as they are, text and dates in quotes: each value with its type, in the order of the columns.

insert-defaults.title: Let the database fill in
intro: An `id` declared as `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is picked by the database when you leave it out: the next free number. Two rows can't have the same id.
A column with a `DEFAULT` gets its default value when you leave it out: an order's status is `'pending'`.
insert-defaults.goal: The order from Gina fails: id 1 is taken. Insert it again, letting the database pick the `id` and the `status`.
hints: Remove `id` and `status` from the list of columns.
Remove their values too: the values must match the columns, one for one.
`INSERT INTO orders (customer, brick_id, quantity, ordered_on) VALUES ('Gina', 3, 20, '2024-11-12');`
insert-defaults.recap: Leave out a column and the database fills it: the next id, the default value, or `NULL`.

update-one.title: Change a row: UPDATE
intro: `UPDATE` changes rows that already exist: `UPDATE` the table, `SET` the column to its new value, and `WHERE` to choose the rows.
Without `WHERE`, every row of the table changes. Write the `WHERE` first, to be safe.
update-one.goal: The yellow Plate 1x6 (id 3) is back: set its stock to 200, and change no other brick.
hints: Replace the `SELECT` with `UPDATE bricks SET ...`.
Keep `WHERE id = 3` to change this brick only.
`UPDATE bricks SET stock = 200 WHERE id = 3;`
update-one.recap: `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE` changes only the rows matched by the `WHERE`.

update-math.title: Compute the new value
intro: The new value can be computed from the current one: `quantity * 2` doubles each row's own quantity. You can use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`.
Each row is computed from its own value, so one query changes many rows differently.
update-math.goal: Raise the price of every red brick by 0.05, from its current price.
hints: `price = 0.50` gives every red brick the same price: compute it from `price` instead.
Add 0.05 to the current price: `price + 0.05`.
`UPDATE bricks SET price = price + 0.05 WHERE color = 'red';`
update-math.recap: `SET price = price + 0.05` computes each row's new value from its own current value.

update-where.title: Ship the late orders
intro: This query has no `WHERE`: it ships every order, even the cancelled ones. A missing `WHERE` is the most common mistake with `UPDATE`.
Use what you learned: conditions joined with `AND`, text and dates between quotes.
update-where.goal: Ship (status `'shipped'`) only the pending orders placed before November 1st, 2024.
hints: Add a `WHERE` with two conditions joined by `AND`.
One condition on `status`, one on `ordered_on` with `<`.
`UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE status = 'pending' AND ordered_on < '2024-11-01';`
update-where.recap: You can read, filter, add and change data: `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `INSERT` and `UPDATE` are the base of every SQL database.
